levels.title: Political philosophy: authority, justice, and justified dissent

units.title: Justifying power among free and equal citizens

lessons.title: Authority is not the same as getting things right
lessons.explanation: A competent government can produce a beneficial decision without yet establishing its right to impose that decision. This lesson moves from the preceding level's evaluation of actions to the justification of institutions that claim authority over people who disagree. Political legitimacy asks whether political power is justified; political obligation asks whether citizens have moral duties to obey. Some theories connect these tightly, while others separate them. Keep the meaning fixed within an argument. The question is not merely whether an official can force compliance, or whether following an instruction would be prudent. It is whether there is an adequate moral basis for that official's rule.
lessons.example: Imagine a skilled engineer who correctly identifies a dangerous bridge. She orders the nearby town to close it and appoints herself permanent mayor. Premise one: avoiding foreseeable injury supplies a strong reason to stop crossing. Premise two: her inspection is reliable evidence of danger. These support temporary avoidance of the bridge. They do not support permanent political authority over unrelated matters. A world in which her warning is correct but her self-appointment is unjustified is a counterexample to the inference from expertise to a general right to rule. Rejecting her mayoral claim therefore need not mean ignoring her warning. Distinguish the reason to act from the proposed source of political obligation.
lessons.question: What does the engineer’s accurate warning establish without further premises?
lessons.answer: A reason to avoid the dangerous bridge, not her permanent right to govern
lessons.distractor: A permanent right to govern because correct advice creates political authority
lessons.correction: The counterexample holds expertise fixed while denying unlimited authority. A further account of authorization or legitimacy is required.

depth.definitions: De facto power is the actual capacity to secure compliance. Normative authority is a claimed moral entitlement to direct conduct. Legitimacy may mean justified coercion, a right to rule, or an authority that generates duties; the assigned reading compares these uses. Consent is an authorization by an agent, not merely behavior consistent with acceptance. Express consent is explicit; tacit consent is conveyed through conduct under conditions that make its significance sufficiently clear. Hypothetical consent concerns what people would agree to, not an agreement they actually made.
depth.mechanism: Consider a consent argument in explicit form. First, valid authorization can sometimes give another person a limited right to make decisions for the authorizer. Second, citizens have validly authorized this institution to make decisions in this domain. Therefore, the institution has that limited authority. The inference exposes the work hidden in the second premise: who authorized what, with which alternatives, and under which informational conditions? Voting for a representative is not straightforwardly consenting to every future directive; refusing to vote is even less obviously consent. Remaining in a country can reflect family responsibilities, lack of admission elsewhere, or inability to move. Such residence does not automatically carry the voluntary meaning of accepting a readily avoidable club membership. A defender can reply that political authority need not rest solely on actual consent: fair procedures, rights protection, or public justification may supply other grounds. That is a change or supplementation of the justificatory argument, not proof that residence was voluntary authorization all along. Consent also has scope limits: consenting to a service is not consenting to unlimited control.
depth.secondExample: Contrast the engineer with a residents' association whose members knowingly sign a revocable agreement authorizing scheduling of a shared workshop. When the association sets a cleaning day within its agreed remit, a member has a consent-based reason to cooperate even if another day would be more convenient. If it then orders the member to change religion, the agreement supplies no such authority. This contrast shows both the strength and limits of consent: genuine authorization can matter, but an authorized institution can exceed its mandate. Real states differ from voluntary associations, so the example isolates a principle rather than proving a theory of state legitimacy.
depth.mistake: A common mistake is to infer that an unjust policy makes every directive of a government nonbinding, or that a beneficial policy validates everything else it does. Both skip distinctions of scope and degree. Ask separately whether the institution is minimally legitimate, whether this policy is just, and whether this person has a duty to comply here. A duty not to injure others can remain even when an institution lacks authority. Conversely, institutional legitimacy does not make each policy morally flawless.
depth.application: Nonblocking practice: a university security office gives a correct evacuation warning and then demands permanent control over student publications. Write an argument granting what the warning establishes while challenging the added power. Model response: the credible hazard supports evacuation; existing emergency authority might independently support the order; neither premise establishes editorial authority after the emergency. Self-review: name the scope of each conclusion, distinguish evidence from authorization, and identify what additional premise the editorial demand needs. For a serious objection, consider whether temporary limits on publishing hazardous location information could protect safety. Explain why that narrower claim still does not establish permanent editorial control.
depth.summary: Authority debates require more than approving or disapproving of a result. Separate competence, actual power, justified coercion, and duties to obey; then specify the domain and duration of the proposed authority. Your earlier countermodel method now tests political inferences: hold beneficial outcomes constant while varying authorization. Next, examine whether receiving cooperative benefits can generate obligations even without consent. That is a different argument and deserves its own premises.

readings.title: Political Legitimacy — sections 1–3
readings.note: Read the conceptual contrasts, the function of legitimacy, and consent under sources of legitimacy. This open scholarly overview compares disputed theories; it is not a single settled definition.

lessons.title: Fair play, public goods, and the unsolicited-benefit objection
lessons.explanation: Political cooperation often supplies benefits that people cannot obtain alone. Does receiving those benefits create a duty to contribute? A fair-play argument answers that it can be unfair to take the benefits of others' restraint while refusing a fair share of its burdens. This differs from consent: the proposed duty arises from reciprocity within cooperation, not necessarily from a promise. It also differs from gratitude, which need not give a benefactor power to dictate repayment. The task is to reconstruct the strongest reciprocity argument without allowing any provider to manufacture obligations merely by delivering something unasked for.
lessons.example: Residents maintain a flood barrier through a transparent, fairly distributed work schedule. A resident knowingly relies on its protection, could take an appropriate shift, but refuses solely because the others will probably maintain it anyway. The fair-play argument identifies a benefit sustained by others' burdens, a reasonable contribution, and deliberate exemption from that burden. Now alter the case: a company installs decorative lights without consultation and sends every resident an enormous bill. Receiving some illumination does not establish liability to any demanded payment. This is a worked counterexample to the universal rule that benefiting always obligates. It does not yet refute the narrower argument about fair, necessary cooperation.
lessons.question: Why does the unwanted lighting bill challenge a simple benefit-based obligation argument?
lessons.answer: Unilaterally supplying a benefit need not authorize the provider to impose its chosen burden
lessons.distractor: No cooperative benefit can ever generate a moral reason to contribute
lessons.correction: The example refutes an unrestricted sufficiency claim. A qualified fair-play argument must still be evaluated on its own conditions.

depth.definitions: A public good, in the standard economic sense used here, is nonexcludable and nonrival: excluding noncontributors is difficult, and one person's enjoyment need not reduce another's. Real goods approximate these properties to different degrees. A free rider benefits from cooperation while avoiding a contribution. Fair play is the moral principle invoked to criticize certain free riding; it is not simply the empirical observation that it occurs. Receiving a benefit and accepting a benefit are distinct: acceptance involves a relevant form of willing uptake.
depth.mechanism: Set out a qualified argument. First, when a cooperative scheme is just, supplies sufficiently important benefits, distributes burdens fairly, and gives participants appropriate standing, beneficiaries may owe a fair contribution. Second, this institution meets those conditions for this benefit and contribution. Therefore, the beneficiary owes that contribution. Each condition limits the conclusion. The unsolicited-benefit objection challenges accounts that omit acceptance or allow providers to choose benefits and costs unilaterally. Fair-play defenders reply that requiring voluntary acceptance for every essential nonexcludable good can make necessary cooperation impossible: protection from pollution cannot be delivered only to consenting lungs. That reply supports taking the importance and unavoidability of some goods seriously, but does not establish any particular financing scheme. A further gap separates a duty to contribute from a general duty to obey every law. A person might owe a reasonable share toward flood prevention while having no fair-play reason to obey a censorship law. The assigned survey presents competing formulations; do not treat the example as a proof that all taxation is justified or all nonpayment excused.
depth.secondExample: A neighborhood cooperative offers a paid garden service that residents can easily decline without losing access to basic necessities. Someone explicitly declines, yet workers mow her garden and demand payment. Here easy exclusion and an actual refusal strengthen the objection to imposed obligation. Compare shared prevention of a dangerous contagious crop pest: a household cannot easily decline the resulting protection. That makes the moral structure different, but fair distribution still matters. If the program burdens the poorest households while exempting its organizers, essential benefits do not by themselves cure the unfair terms. Importance, consent, and fairness each do different argumentative work.
depth.mistake: Do not label everyone who fails to contribute a free rider in the blameworthy sense. Someone may lack capacity, reasonably dispute the allocation, or be excluded from the scheme's supposed benefits. Diagnose the mechanism: inability is not strategic exemption, and a protest against discriminatory terms is not automatically an attempt to exploit cooperation. Conversely, saying that one's personal contribution would not change the outcome does not answer a fair-play argument, whose concern includes the fairness of benefiting from others' compliance.
depth.application: Nonblocking practice: a shared emergency radio network is funded by equal household fees, although some households cannot afford them. Draft a conditional argument for contribution and an objection to the fee structure. Model response: reliable common protection can ground reciprocity, but an equal fee may not be a fair burden when capacities differ; revise the financing before inferring a duty to pay that amount. Self-review should locate the benefit, explain why individual exclusion matters, identify a fair burden rather than assume it, and separate support for the network from blanket political obedience. Add the strongest reply: contribution exemptions require a sustainable alternative, not merely a morally attractive announcement.
depth.summary: Fair play is strongest as a bounded argument about justified cooperative terms, not a magical conversion of any benefit into debt. Test receipt against acceptance, essential goods against optional services, and fair contribution against obedience to unrelated commands. This prepares the next lesson: people may dispute which cooperative terms are fair, so institutions must explain how their reasons address citizens who hold different comprehensive views.

readings.title: Political Obligation — section 4.2, Fair Play
readings.note: Read Fair Play in Contemporary Theories, comparing receipt and acceptance of benefits and objections to general political obligation. Use Conceptual Matters to distinguish legal from moral obligations.

lessons.title: Public reason without pretending everyone agrees
lessons.explanation: People can disagree conscientiously about religion, ultimate value, and a good life while sharing political institutions. Public-reason theories ask what kinds of justification are appropriate when those institutions exercise power over everyone. The aim is not to prove that disputed worldviews are false. It is to explain coercive terms to citizens regarded as free and equal rather than merely declaring that the majority's worldview wins. Theories differ about which decisions require public justification, whose perspectives count, and whether citizens must share the same reasons. Learning these differences prevents public reason from becoming a vague synonym for polite discussion.
lessons.example: A council proposes equal access to public meeting rooms. One member supports it because equal citizenship requires it; another because hospitality is a religious duty; a third because open association supports inquiry. They may converge on the same rule without agreeing on its deepest ground. A consensus-style public justification seeks sufficient reasons they can share, such as equal civic standing. A convergence approach can allow different sufficient reasons for each person. Now imagine that the rule instead privileges one faith because its revelation is asserted to be uniquely authoritative. People outside that faith have not yet received a justification addressed to them merely because the assertion was spoken at a public meeting.
lessons.question: What distinguishes convergence from a shared-reason requirement?
lessons.answer: Different citizens may have different sufficient reasons for the same rule
lessons.distractor: A rule needs no adequate justification to those subject to it
lessons.correction: Convergence changes the structure of justification, not the demand that justification reach each relevant citizen.

depth.definitions: A comprehensive doctrine concerns broad moral, religious, or philosophical commitments, rather than only shared political arrangements. Public reason is a normative constraint on justification, not simply speech made in public. Reasonable pluralism names the persistence of different reasonable views under free institutions; it does not mean every conceivable demand deserves equal authority. Consensus accounts require an appropriate common justificatory basis. Convergence accounts permit different adequate reasons to support a common rule. Neither means that every actual person must enthusiastically endorse the outcome.
depth.mechanism: A central argument begins with equal standing: citizens are not natural subordinates of one another. Coercive rules therefore require justification that addresses each as a participant, not only as an obstacle. Since reasonable disagreement persists, appeal to the truth of one comprehensive doctrine may not supply the needed reciprocal justification. Hence proponents impose constraints on political reasons or on their acceptability. Critics challenge the move from equality to those constraints: if a moral claim is true, why exclude it simply because someone disputes it? Others argue that restrictions burden religious citizens more heavily, or conceal controversial liberal assumptions under the word reasonable. A defender can answer that public political values are not value-free and that the requirement need not govern all private association or all public discussion. But that reply must specify scope rather than silently restricting any unpopular speech. Another objection concerns convergence: agreeing on a rule for incompatible reasons can leave citizens without a shared basis for interpreting it later. The reply is that plural reasons can still justify a rule to each affected person, though institutional interpretation remains a further problem. These are substantive disputes, not defects cured by courtesy alone.
depth.secondExample: Consider protecting a town's drinking water. A religious group invokes stewardship, a secular group invokes health, and local residents invoke equal security. This may satisfy a convergence test, but the factual premise that a restriction protects water still needs evidence. A different case exposes the limit: every group favors a different restrictive rule and none has sufficient reason for the others' proposal. Merely collecting sincere views does not manufacture a publicly justified policy. Investigators may find less restrictive alternatives, decision procedures may resolve action temporarily, or a public-reason account may judge some coercion unjustified. Agreement on a desired goal is not agreement on every means.
depth.mistake: The diagnostic mistake is to treat public reason as either complete unanimity or complete neutrality about value. A rule can remain controversial after an adequate justification, and equal standing is already a moral commitment. Conversely, labeling a reason secular does not automatically make it acceptable to everyone: an elaborate secular doctrine can be as disputed as a religious one. Ask which reasons are doing the justificatory work, whom they address, and why the proposed audience restrictions themselves are defensible.
depth.application: Nonblocking practice: draft a justification for a common examination timetable that accommodates serious observance conflicts without granting any group control over everyone else's schedule. Model response: access to education and fair opportunities to demonstrate learning justify reasonable alternative sittings, subject to genuine scheduling and integrity constraints. People may support those values from different doctrines. Self-review: identify a shared political value, a factual feasibility assumption, a reasonable objection, and a revision if accommodation creates an unfair disadvantage. Then write a convergence version using different sufficient reasons. Explain why agreement about the result does not settle whether the consensus and convergence theories are equivalent.
depth.summary: Public reason distinguishes being convinced that a policy is right from justifying coercion to others with equal standing. Compare consensus and convergence without erasing either truth or disagreement. Use the earlier is–ought distinction to expose both factual and normative premises in public arguments. Next, study a candidate limit on coercion: preventing harm, while refusing to confuse mere disapproval with harm.

readings.title: Public Reason — Why Public Reason?, Structure, and Objections
readings.note: Read the discussion of consensus and convergence under Structure, then the objections concerning exclusion and antidemocratic implications. The scholarly entry distinguishes families of views.

visual.title: Public reason without pretending everyone agrees: reasoning map
visual.description: Compare two routes to justifying a common rule: shared sufficient reasons and distinct sufficient reasons for different citizens. Neither route requires identical comprehensive beliefs.

lessons.title: The harm principle: necessary condition, not blank permission
lessons.explanation: A community's dislike of a way of life is not yet a justification for coercively stopping it. Mill's harm principle is a famous attempt to distinguish protection of others from paternalism and moralistic control. In its familiar formulation, preventing harm to others can justify interference with a competent adult's liberty; that person's own good alone is insufficient. Interpretations of Mill remain contested, including how this principle relates to utility and how harm should be understood. Use the principle as an argument requiring analysis, not a slogan that automatically settles every speech, safety, or public-health dispute.
lessons.example: A town proposes banning an unpopular style of dress because observers find it offensive. The argument supplies disapproval but no established injury to a protected interest. Contrast a shop releasing smoke that damages neighbors' property. The smoke case introduces a harm-to-others rationale missing from the dress case. Yet it does not follow that closing every shop forever is justified. Repairing equipment may prevent the harm while restricting liberty less. Reconstruct the logic: harm prevention may be a necessary basis for coercion in this framework; the existence of harm does not make every proposed intervention proportionate or effective. This distinction reuses necessary and sufficient conditions from the foundational course.
lessons.question: What follows from establishing harmful smoke in the shop example?
lessons.answer: A possible harm-prevention rationale that still requires an effective and proportionate response
lessons.distractor: Permission for any restriction officials choose to impose
lessons.correction: Showing a relevant harm answers one justificatory question. Necessity, alternatives, effectiveness, and burdens remain open.

depth.definitions: Paternalism restricts someone for their own good, especially against their wishes. Legal moralism supports coercion on grounds of moral wrongness beyond independently established harm to others. Offense includes distress or disgust that is not automatically the relevant sort of harm. A self-regarding act is one whose relevant effects concern the agent; this classification is disputed because lives are interdependent. Soft paternalist interventions check whether conduct is informed and voluntary; hard paternalism restricts even adequately informed, voluntary choices for the chooser's welfare.
depth.mechanism: Mill's case for liberty is not indifference to how people live. Experiments in living, development of judgment, and protection against mistaken social authority can support leaving people room to choose. The argument challenges a transition from believing someone's choice unwise to claiming a right to force another choice. A strong objection notes that apparently private choices have effects on families, institutions, and shared resources. If any remote cost counts as harm sufficient for interference, the principle loses its protective function. A defender must distinguish effects relevant to others' rights or important interests from mere dislike and attenuated burdens, and must still compare alternatives. Another objection concerns unequal bargaining conditions: formally voluntary conduct may occur amid dependency or coercive threats. Calling the decision self-regarding before examining those conditions begs the question. Conversely, assuming that choosing badly proves incapacity also begs the question. Mill's historical restrictions on the principle's application, including exclusionary assumptions about peoples he considered unready for liberty, require criticism rather than silent endorsement. The contemporary constructed cases here concern competent adults and do not import those exclusions as justified.
depth.secondExample: Imagine a person approaching a bridge whose support has visibly failed but who has not seen the warning. Briefly alerting or stopping them to establish informed choice differs from permanently forbidding all risky travel on the ground that officials know the best life. In the first case, the intervention can protect the conditions of agency; in the second, officials override agency for welfare even after the relevant facts are understood. Neither example settles every emergency practice. It shows why information, voluntariness, urgency, and the scope of interference matter separately. The reasoning is philosophical analysis, not a legal instruction for physically restraining someone.
depth.mistake: Avoid the shortcut that every emotional response is mere offense and therefore morally irrelevant. Threats, harassment, and intimidation can impair important interests or effective liberty; their analysis requires details. The opposite shortcut is that any reported distress authorizes censorship. Ask what conduct occurred, how it affects others, what evidence supports the link, and which response addresses that link. Disagreement over the definition of harm must be argued explicitly rather than hidden inside a label that already assumes the desired verdict.
depth.application: Nonblocking practice: a housing cooperative proposes banning all evening music after complaints about sleeplessness. Write a narrow policy analysis rather than choosing between unlimited noise and unlimited silence. Model response: repeated noise that prevents neighbors from sleeping may supply a harm-based reason; measure the relevant disturbance, compare quiet hours and sound reduction, and preserve harmless use. Self-review: distinguish injury from dislike of the genre, identify a causal premise, state the least restrictive feasible alternative you considered, and name a fact that would change your recommendation. Address the objection that enforcement could selectively burden an unpopular cultural group even under apparently neutral wording.
depth.summary: Liberty analysis combines normative limits with factual inquiry. Identify who is protected, which interest is threatened, whether the decision is informed, and whether interference is justified in kind and degree. A harm rationale is not proof of an intervention's success. The next lesson applies the same separation of evidence and authority to democratic decisions: expertise matters, but it does not by itself determine who should possess political power.

readings.title: Mill’s Moral and Political Philosophy — section 3, Mill’s Liberalism
readings.note: Read the discussion of liberty, paternalism, offense, harm, and limits on state authority. This secondary overview explains interpretive disputes rather than presenting a contemporary legal test.

lessons.title: Democratic equality and epistemic authority
lessons.explanation: Why should citizens share political power when they differ in relevant knowledge? One defense of democracy emphasizes better decisions: participation gathers dispersed information and subjects claims to criticism. Another emphasizes equal standing: people who must live under common rules should not be treated as political inferiors. These defenses can cooperate, but they can also conflict. This lesson evaluates proposals to replace public decision-making with expert rule without pretending either voters or experts are infallible. It extends the earlier study of testimony and source independence from individual belief to collective institutions.
lessons.example: A city must choose a flood-defense plan. Hydrologists understand water flows; residents know which routes are usable during evacuations; elected officials must justify whose property and access are burdened. Expertise in forecasting does not alone identify a fair distribution of risk. A proposal to let hydrologists permanently govern every city matter therefore needs an additional argument. Conversely, allowing a majority vote to decide the height of a measured river does not turn preference into evidence. A defensible division of labor gives technical claims accountable expert scrutiny and makes value-laden tradeoffs subject to publicly justified decision procedures. It does not split facts and values so neatly that either group can ignore the other.
lessons.question: Why do many votes copying one report not establish independent corroboration?
lessons.answer: The judgments share one evidential source despite coming from different voters
lessons.distractor: Public participation can never contribute relevant knowledge
lessons.correction: Dependence weakens this epistemic argument, not every argument for democracy or every form of citizen knowledge.

depth.definitions: An instrumental defense values a procedure because it tends to produce good outcomes. A noninstrumental defense assigns significance to the procedure itself, such as expressing political equality. Epistemic democracy emphasizes the truth-tracking or problem-solving capacities of democratic institutions. Epistocracy assigns political authority partly on the basis of knowledge or competence. Expertise is domain-specific: competence in engineering is not automatic competence in moral judgment, local experience, or every other science. Political equality does not require believing everyone has identical information.
depth.mechanism: An epistemic argument can take this form: inclusive participation can reveal relevant dispersed information; deliberation can expose errors; institutions that preserve those advantages may make better decisions than insulated rulers. The qualifications matter. If everyone repeats one misleading report, adding voters adds repetition rather than independent evidence. If powerful participants intimidate others, nominal inclusion need not produce informational inclusion. Mathematical jury arguments likewise rely on substantive assumptions about competence and independence, not just the number of people voting. No probability calculation is needed to see the failure of independence when all judgments copy one source. Critics of democracy point to ignorance and manipulation. A defender should address these with evidence institutions, accessible deliberation, and accountability rather than denying their possibility. Critics of expert rule ask who selects the experts and whether selection reproduces class or ideological advantage. Expertise can help identify means while leaving contestable ends unresolved. Equal standing supplies a further objection to permanent rule by a purportedly superior class even when that class is technically skilled. Whether that objection is decisive depends on the theory of legitimacy being defended; it is not established merely by calling the scheme elitist.
depth.secondExample: Consider a workplace vote on ventilation. Workers consistently report headaches in a room that an engineer inspected only while empty. Their testimony identifies a possible mismatch between test conditions and actual use. This is not proof of a particular cause, but it is a reason to retest during occupancy. Now reverse the asymmetry: an accurate technical warning about an invisible hazard is dismissed because most workers cannot smell anything. Here participation without suitable scientific input fails. The contrasting examples show that institutional design should connect different kinds of knowledge and provide ways to challenge both credentialed authority and confident majorities.
depth.mistake: A frequent mistake is to treat a fair vote as evidence that its substantive outcome must be correct. Another is to treat a technically correct answer as sufficient justification for disenfranchising those affected. Diagnose which premise is missing: reliability concerns how beliefs connect to truth; legitimacy concerns how power is justified. Democratic institutions may deserve reform when unreliable, and legitimate decisions may still warrant criticism. Neither claim implies that truth is created by a ballot or that disagreement with experts always reflects irrationality.
depth.application: Nonblocking practice: design a decision process for relocating a noisy transit depot. Model response: commission independently reviewable noise and travel studies, invite affected workers and residents to challenge assumptions, publish feasible alternatives, decide through accountable representatives, and create a review mechanism if predictions fail. Self-review: include at least one safeguard against dependent evidence, one against exclusion, and one against indefinitely postponing a necessary decision. Steelman the expert-rule objection that lengthy consultation wastes scarce time; reply by distinguishing an urgent temporary measure from permanent removal of accountability. This institutional design task tests reasoning, not professional competence in governance or engineering.
depth.summary: Democracy's epistemic and equality-based arguments answer different questions. Seek institutions that make evidence answerable to criticism while giving affected citizens genuine standing. The completed unit now offers several possible grounds and limits of political authority: consent, fair cooperation, public justification, liberty, and democratic equality. The next unit asks what those institutions should distribute and how to recognize injustice that persists even under formally fair procedures.

readings.title: Democracy — sections 2–4, justification, authority, and participation
readings.note: Compare epistemic justifications with equality and public-justification arguments, then read the authority discussion. Jury-theorem applications require assumptions; this lesson makes no numerical forecast.
